question: What is the classical clinical definition of puerperal pyrexia?

answers.text: Temperature ≥37.5°C at any time in the first 10 days after delivery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 37.5°C is below the classic threshold, and the time window is not 10 days. The definition requires a higher temperature and a specific time window to distinguish from the post-delivery physiological temperature rise.

answers.text: Temperature ≥38°C on any two of the first 10 days postpartum (excluding the first 24 hours)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Puerperal pyrexia is classically defined as a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or above, occurring on any TWO of the first 10 days postpartum (excluding the first 24 hours). The exclusion of the first 24 hours avoids including the transient physiological temperature rise from labour.
38.5°C is too high a threshold, and 48 hours is too narrow a window. This would miss most cases of puerperal infection that present between days 3–7.

answers.text: Temperature ≥38°C on any day within 6 weeks of delivery, including the first 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The first 24 hours are specifically excluded to avoid false positives from the physiological post-labour temperature elevation. The window is 10 days, not 6 weeks (though infection can occur throughout the puerperium).

overallFeedback.feedback: The classic definition: 38°C or above on any TWO of the first 10 days postpartum, excluding the first 24 hours. Memorise this threshold and the time window.
Correct. Puerperal pyrexia = 38°C on any 2 of days 1–10 postpartum (excluding day 0). This is a standard examination definition.
